problem: The direction of merged mining is reversed. Namecoin is the auxiliary (child) chain and Bitcoin is the parent chain: the hash of the Namecoin block is committed inside the Bitcoin coinbase transaction, not the other way round. As written, the miner is asked to put the hash of a Bitcoin block B into a Namecoin header, but B's hash does not exist until B's nonce is found, so the stated steps cannot be carried out. Saying 'submit the same proof to Namecoin' also hides that the proof is the Bitcoin block header plus its coinbase.
fix: Steps: 1) Build a Namecoin candidate block N. 2) Hash N and put that hash into the coinbase transaction of a Bitcoin candidate block B. 3) Search for a nonce that makes B meet Bitcoin's target. 4) Broadcast B to Bitcoin; the miner earns Bitcoin. 5) If B's hash also meets Namecoin's target, submit B's header and coinbase (the proof) together with N to Namecoin; N is then a valid Namecoin block. Rule for students: the chain whose hash is committed is the child; the chain that carries the commitment in its coinbase is the parent.

problem: 'Three transaction forms exist: transparent to transparent, transparent to shielded, and shielded to shielded' is wrong. Zcash has four forms; shielded to transparent (z to t) is missing, and it is exactly the form students confuse with full privacy.
fix: Four transaction forms exist: transparent to transparent (t to t), transparent to shielded (t to z), shielded to shielded (z to z) and shielded to transparent (z to t). Only z to z hides sender, receiver and amount; t to z hides the receiver and amount but the sender is public.

problem: The ledger records only ZEC amounts; a rupee value never appears on chain. Saying 'the public sees ... the ₹6,000 equivalent' can make a student think the rupee figure is part of the transaction data.
fix: The public sees the sender, the receiver and the amount 1.5 ZEC; the ₹6,000 is only your conversion at ₹4,000 per ZEC, not data on the ledger. Same wording in the Q3 answer for ₹4,000.
